title: Useful heat engines that are simultaneously efficient, powerful, and steady

concept.text: The target is a finite, macroscopic heat engine that converts heat into work with three properties at the same operating point: efficiency close to the Carnot ceiling set by its hot and cold reservoirs, useful net power per unit volume, and output steady enough to drive a mechanical or electrical load. High efficiency alone is insufficient if the engine produces work arbitrarily slowly; high average power alone is insufficient if large fluctuations make that output difficult to use. This is a proposed joint laboratory capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

The underlying challenge is a trade-off with a defined mathematical scope. For thermodynamically consistent steady engines described by discrete-state Markov dynamics or overdamped Langevin dynamics, the documented power–efficiency–constancy bound implies that approaching Carnot efficiency while retaining nonvanishing power requires a diverging long-time power-fluctuation intensity. This limiting result does not prohibit every favorable combination at a finite distance from Carnot. An apparatus meeting demanding but finite efficiency, power, and stability thresholds would not necessarily violate the bound or require its dynamical assumptions to fail.

significance.text: A practical realization would establish a major heat-to-work conversion capability: retaining useful throughput and usable output while losing relatively little of the conversion efficiency permitted by the reservoir temperatures. Its significance would lie in demonstrating all three properties together under realistic resource accounting. A microscopic cycle or an idealized model reaching Carnot efficiency only through an infinite-system limit would provide scientific insight, but would not by itself establish this macroscopic capability.

Conditional engineering assessment: such an engine could change the design options available for power generation or heat-powered transport if its advantages survived practical heat exchange, auxiliary energy consumption, durability requirements, and control under changing loads. The supplied evidence does not quantify an economy-wide benefit or establish how much fuel exergy is currently lost specifically to finite-speed operation and output fluctuations. Benefits to refrigeration would require a separate demonstration of cooling performance and energy costs; they do not follow automatically from a successful heat-engine experiment.

The advance would concern performance below or approaching the Carnot ceiling, rather than replacing that ceiling. Carnot efficiency already provides a universal efficiency limit for a two-reservoir heat engine under the relevant thermodynamic conditions. Bounds on performance at finite power, including their dependence on dynamics, system size, and fluctuations, address additional questions. A general theory of those bounds and a useful laboratory engine are distinct objectives; the supplied record does not justify ranking the theoretical objective as intrinsically weaker.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a working substance and engine architecture that jointly sustain near-Carnot net efficiency, useful finite power density, and load-relevant stability at finite size. The theoretical difficulty is to understand how the quantities entering existing bounds behave as performance improves: whether gains in efficiency require falling throughput, increasing fluctuations, growing system resources, or some combination. Favorable finite performance remains a meaningful target within the bounds, so identifying a loophole in their assumptions is not a prerequisite.

Collective working substances offer one theoretical direction, but their limiting advantages must be translated into finite apparatus performance. The Liang, Ma, Busiello, and De Los Rios manuscript describes a minimal model whose efficiency at maximum power approaches Carnot as a degeneracy-related entropy parameter s tends to infinity, corresponding to an infinite-system limit. Its optimization assumes a constant characteristic cycle time. A practical advance would therefore need to establish how cycle time, heat transfer, output power per volume, and fluctuations actually scale when the collective or degeneracy resource is physically implemented.

Engineering synthesis: the apparatus must exchange heat rapidly enough to deliver useful power while keeping irreversible losses sufficiently small, and must retain its advantage after controls and other auxiliary demands are counted. Output stability must also survive coupling to a real load. Any buffering or regulation used to smooth the output should be included in the apparatus boundary and resource account, so that external storage or control does not silently substitute for the engine's own demonstrated performance.

Constancy is itself a measurement challenge. The documented steady-engine theory characterizes fluctuations through the long-time growth of work variance, while an application experiences power over finite time windows. Because both mean accumulated work and its variance can grow linearly with observation time, a relative standard deviation without a specified averaging window can obscure substantial fluctuations at shorter times. A convincing engine must therefore connect its fluctuation statistics to the response times and bandwidth of the intended load.

current_state.text: Shiraishi, Saito, and Tasaki's 2016 work is identified in the supplied research as Physical Review Letters 117, 190601, dated 31 October 2016, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.190601. Later papers in the supplied review discuss it as a foundational finite-power efficiency result. However, its original article was not captured for that review. Its exact theorem assumptions and the earlier text's direct quotation therefore cannot be independently established from the supplied original-source material; the attribution has indirect support and should not be treated as a directly checked theorem statement.

Pietzonka and Seifert, Physical Review Letters 120, 190602 (2018), derive a joint power–efficiency–constancy trade-off for steady engines operating between two heat baths. The full paper and supplemental material were available to the supplied review. Their result applies to thermodynamically consistent discrete-state Markov dynamics and overdamped Langevin dynamics: maintaining finite or increasing power as efficiency approaches Carnot requires the long-time power-fluctuation intensity to diverge. The result concerns this limiting behavior within the stated classes, rather than a blanket impossibility of simultaneously favorable finite performance.

Zhai and coworkers, Physical Review E 107, L042101, published 18 April 2023, report an experimental finite-time Carnot cycle using sealed dry air as the working substance. Their abstract reports a power–efficiency trade-off and an efficiency at maximum power of (0.524 ± 0.034) η_C, where η_C is the Carnot efficiency for the reservoirs. The supplied review had access to the abstract, but not the article body, figures, or methods. This supports the dated reported result and its numerical value; it does not establish the proposed joint performance, practical power density, or output-fluctuation statistics.

The supplied manuscript by Liang, Ma, Busiello, and De Los Rios presents a theoretical minimal model in which efficiency at maximum power approaches Carnot as s, a degeneracy-related entropy parameter, tends to infinity. The manuscript associates this behavior with the thermodynamic limit of infinite system size and assumes a constant characteristic cycle time during optimization. Its finite-size discussion retains a finite trade-off prefactor and does not establish Carnot efficiency at finite power for a finite engine. This is a theoretical limiting result, not an experimental demonstration of useful power density and constancy.

The Liang manuscript identifies a universal power–efficiency trade-off for collective engines, and the connection between engine performance and many-body phase transitions, as open questions at the time of writing. The supplied research attributes the work to Physical Review Letters 134, 027101, dated 13 January 2025, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.027101. The supplied review verified the manuscript's title and authors but could not internally confirm that publication attribution. Supplemental derivations referenced by the manuscript were also not supplied, limiting assessment of its complete supporting argument.

Evidence boundary: these historical results motivate the target but do not establish whether any macroscopic engine had met the proposed joint test by 1 November 2026. The supplied record contains no bounded freshness-search results supporting either a claim of continued absence or a claim of achievement. That gap does not invalidate the supported experiments or theoretical results, and it does not establish that the collective-engine questions remain open at that later date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: use one finite apparatus with specified hot- and cold-reservoir temperatures and a declared system boundary. At the same operating point, demonstrate net efficiency above 0.9 η_C, a preregistered minimum useful net power per unit volume, and the proposed stability threshold. Define the heat and work measurements, auxiliary energy accounting, apparatus volume, and uncertainties before the test. The 0.9 threshold and the requirement to choose a useful power-density threshold are proposed benchmarks, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Efficiency above 0.9 η_C with useful power density and stability

completion_criteria.text: Proposed power comparison: require net mean power at least equal to a preregistered baseline measured on the same apparatus at the Curzon–Ahlborn efficiency, if that operating point is accessible. Specify how the operating point is selected and which resources, reservoir conditions, and apparatus settings are held fixed. Do not assume that the Curzon–Ahlborn efficiency identifies this apparatus's maximum-power point. If it is inaccessible, declare and justify an alternative baseline before evaluating the result. An unusually weak baseline cannot replace the separate useful-power-density requirement.
completion_criteria.label: Net mean power matches or exceeds the preregistered baseline

completion_criteria.text: Proposed constancy test: require a relative standard deviation of delivered power below 10 percent using a preregistered averaging window and measurement bandwidth appropriate to the intended load. Specify a continuous run duration long enough to characterize correlations, slow drift, and the apparatus's relevant operating cycles. Publish efficiency, mean power, time-resolved output, fluctuation statistics, and their uncertainties together. Include a long-time fluctuation characterization where applicable so the finite-window measurement can be compared with the theoretical notion of constancy.
completion_criteria.label: Delivered power relative standard deviation stays below 10 percent

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirements: disclose apparatus size, finite working-substance resources, any degeneracy parameter, operating protocol, auxiliary costs, load coupling, and output-smoothing equipment. Repeat the joint measurement across runs and seek independent reproduction using a sufficiently detailed protocol. Test a declared range of reservoir temperatures and loads to establish practical boundaries. Such finite tests would establish the breadth demonstrated by that apparatus; they would not prove universal performance across working substances, dynamics, or operating conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated joint measurements disclose resources and establish tested operating boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: THR-05, “A size-extensive quantum advantage in thermodynamic performance,” is the closest alternative route. Quantum resources might help a working substance achieve the joint engine target, but a quantum advantage and a macroscopic engine with near-Carnot efficiency, useful power density, and steady output are different demonstrations. THR-02 does not require a quantum mechanism, and an advantage under THR-05 would need separate evidence that it delivers THR-02's practical performance. Only THR-05's title was supplied, so its detailed requirements cannot be compared here.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-04, “Bulk electronic heat–charge decoupling sufficient for engine-class solid-state conversion,” concerns a material-level route that could contribute to a heat engine. THR-07, “Synthetic chemomechanical engines whose efficiency approaches biological molecular motors,” concerns conversion through synthetic molecular machinery. Both overlap with efficient energy conversion, but their stated targets do not by themselves establish THR-02's simultaneous macroscopic power density and constancy near the relevant Carnot limit. Each remains a distinct innovation.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-01, “A computable thermodynamic potential for far-from-equilibrium continuum transport,” THR-11, “Operational temperature and entropy for far-from-equilibrium matter,” and THR-12, “Predictive thermodynamic design of far-from-equilibrium chemical reaction networks,” could provide tools for describing or designing unconventional working substances. Their central targets are predictive or operational thermodynamic descriptions, whereas THR-02 requires measured engine performance. Likewise, a general finite-power efficiency bound is a related theoretical objective, but it is not an additional roster entry or a substitute for the joint apparatus demonstration.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-03, “General-purpose digital computation near the Landauer scale,” and THR-08, “Equilibrium sampling computers operating near thermal energy per sample,” also connect thermodynamic limits with useful throughput. Their outputs are computational operations or samples rather than net mechanical or electrical work. Their limiting energy scales and performance tests therefore remain distinct from a heat engine's reservoir-dependent efficiency, power density, and output fluctuations.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-06, “A single-absorber solar converter that uses non-thermal carriers to pass the detailed-balance limit,” shares the goal of improved energy conversion but concerns a specified solar-conversion limit and non-thermal carriers. Passing that limit would not establish near-Carnot performance for a two-reservoir heat engine, and THR-02 would not establish THR-06's solar-converter capability.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-09, “A thermodynamic design theory of self-replicators, confirmed by a predicted non-biological replicator,” and THR-10, “A laboratory measurement of the Unruh temperature,” share a broad thermodynamic setting but have different central outputs: predicted replication and a temperature measurement, respectively. Neither title supplies a direct route to THR-02's joint engine capability. These comparisons are limited to the supplied roster titles and do not presume additional evidence for those entries.

brief.title: Heat engines with efficient, strong, steady output
possible: A generator or heat-powered vehicle could turn heat into useful work close to the Carnot limit: the highest efficiency allowed by its hot and cold temperatures. A practical-sized engine would deliver useful power for its size, steadily enough to drive a mechanical or electrical load.
why: For power generation and heat-powered transport, this would expand the options for getting useful work from heat. The gain would come from combining high efficiency with strong, usable output, counting the energy used by controls and other supporting equipment.

sources.showed: This is theoretical work on the trade-off between power and efficiency in heat engines.
sources.cited_for: It supports the theoretical background on efficiency at finite power.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a practical-sized engine combining near-limit efficiency, useful power, and steady output.

sources.showed: They proved a trade-off for broad classes of engines running continuously between hot and cold reservoirs. As efficiency approaches the Carnot limit, retaining power requires increasingly large output fluctuations.

sources.not_established: An infinite-system result does not demonstrate the combined performance in a finite engine with realistic heat transfer and output fluctuations.

shown: Zhai and colleagues demonstrated a dry-air engine whose efficiency at maximum power reached about half the Carnot limit. Liang and colleagues developed a model that approaches the limit at maximum power, but only as system size becomes infinite. Neither result establishes the full practical capability.
missing: A finite engine must combine near-limit efficiency, useful net power per unit volume, and steady output at the same operating point.
Fast heat exchange must preserve efficiency after the energy costs of controls and supporting equipment are counted.
Delivered output must stay steady when connected to a real load, with any storage or smoothing equipment included in the resource account.

milestones.label: Efficiency, useful power, and stability meet their thresholds together
milestones.explanation: A finite apparatus would have to exceed 90% of the Carnot limit while meeting predeclared useful net power per volume and stability thresholds, with auxiliary costs counted. This establishes the combined capability.

milestones.label: Net power matches or exceeds the predeclared comparison
milestones.explanation: Net power would have to match a predeclared same-apparatus comparison at the Curzon–Ahlborn reference efficiency, or a justified alternative if inaccessible. This tests retained output under controlled resources.

milestones.label: Delivered power varies little on timescales the load needs
milestones.explanation: Delivered power's standard deviation, its typical spread around the average, would have to stay below 10% of that average over predeclared load-relevant timescales during a sustained run. This tests whether the load gets usable output.

milestones.label: Repeated joint tests establish resources and operating boundaries
milestones.explanation: Joint measurements would have to repeat with resources and costs disclosed, independent reproduction sought, and a declared range of temperatures and loads tested. This establishes reproducibility and the apparatus's operating boundaries.

uncertain: The minimum useful power per unit volume and the timescales needed to judge stability still need to be chosen for a concrete test.
It remains unclear how collective effects scale alongside cycle time, heat exchange, supporting energy costs, and output fluctuations in a finite engine.
The efficiency and stability thresholds are proposed benchmarks, rather than established standards.

page.title: Power–efficiency–constancy optimization in heat engines
page.definition: A finite macroscopic heat engine simultaneously meets specified limits on conversion efficiency, net power per apparatus volume, and output fluctuations. Efficiency is measured relative to the Carnot ceiling, η_C = 1 − T_c/T_h, where the reservoir temperatures are in kelvins; constancy means small output fluctuations.

goal.need: A DOE assessment published in March 2008 distinguished discarded industrial heat from its smaller theoretical work potential. Converting more of that potential requires efficiency at finite output power. For steady engines described by thermodynamically consistent discrete-state Markov or overdamped Langevin dynamics, the published power–efficiency–constancy bound also constrains output fluctuations.

figures.note: One TBtu is 10¹² British thermal units. Exhaust heat and work potential use a reference temperature of 25 °C. Work potential is a theoretical upper bound, not measured electricity production; these estimates cover selected processes.

completion.title: Independent tests reproduce a finite engine's joint efficiency, power-density, and load-stability performance.
completion.criterion: Independent replication of one finite macroscopic two-reservoir engine at one operating point: net η/η_C ≥ α, net mean power/apparatus volume ≥ p_min (W m⁻³), and delivered-power coefficient of variation ≤ c_max over a specified load-relevant averaging window, bandwidth, and run duration. Controls, auxiliaries, and output buffers belong to the apparatus boundary. External values for α, p_min, c_max, the measurement conditions, and the size cutoff were not located. These symbols identify missing acceptance limits; this fallback is not yet an executable pass/fail test.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external body was identified as setting a joint macroscopic acceptance test.
completion.basis: Searches covered the supplied papers, the 2025 thermodynamics roadmap, DOE/ARPA-E and CORDIS programme targets, and public ASME PTC 46 and ISO 8528-5 descriptions. No joint numerical acceptance test was located. The mathematical trade-offs constrain performance within stated dynamics; they do not define engineering acceptance limits. The fallback retains the joint physical demonstration and leaves unsupported cutoffs unassigned.

milestones.title: A finite-time laboratory heat-engine cycle delivers positive mean work.
milestones.criterion: At the working-substance boundary, mean extracted work per cycle is positive and the cycle duration is finite, so mean output power is positive. Martínez et al.'s manuscript revised on 30 July 2015 reports this behavior for one optically trapped colloidal particle, with ensemble averages over 50 s. A noisy electrostatic force emulates a thermal bath. This is a working-substance demonstration; it does not establish positive net power after the optical and electrical apparatus costs.
milestones.set_by: Stochastic-thermodynamics engine/heat-pump sign convention, applied experimentally by Martínez et al. in Brownian Carnot engine.

milestones.title: A finite-time heat-engine protocol reaches positive maximum mean power over its allowed cycle timings.
milestones.criterion: For fixed reservoir conditions and a specified timing domain, the protocol attains P_max = max P > 0. Zhai et al., published on 18 April 2023, report eight repeats per operating point. At T_h = 319.2 K and T_c = 308.2 K, the reported maximizing stroke times are 13.32 s and 12.60 s. Across temperature combinations, the fitted efficiency at maximum power is (0.524 ± 0.034)η_C. The protocol infers the adiabatic strokes from separate isothermal runs; it does not demonstrate a complete load-driving engine or apparatus-level net efficiency.
milestones.set_by: Efficiency-at-maximum-power convention of finite-time thermodynamics; Zhai et al. apply timing optimization to a sealed-dry-air Carnot-cycle protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: Optimization of the cycle for maximum power is achieved

milestones.title: A finite macroscopic prototype meets all three joint limits in one laboratory.
milestones.criterion: At one operating point, one prototype satisfies η/η_C ≥ α, P_net/V ≥ p_min, and delivered-power coefficient of variation ≤ c_max under the specified load and measurement conditions, counting auxiliaries and buffering, before independent replication. External numerical limits remain unassigned. Liang et al., published on 13 January 2025, instead provide a model approaching Carnot efficiency at maximum power as its degeneracy-related entropy parameter diverges, corresponding to infinite system size; the optimization holds characteristic cycle time fixed. That result supplies no finite-prototype pass.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback for the demonstration preceding independent replication; no external joint prototype-qualification criterion was located.

not_found: No external numerical specification jointly defining the required Carnot-efficiency fraction, net volumetric power, and load-relevant constancy was located.
No externally adopted macroscopic size cutoff or joint prototype-qualification stage was located.
The full normative texts of ASME PTC 46 and ISO 8528-5 were not accessible; their public descriptions were checked.
No independently replicated macroscopic demonstration meeting an externally specified joint test was located; the missing acceptance limits prevent an achievement determination.
